prompt: A logistics company's strategy opens: "Diagnosis: our costs are too high, our app is slow, hiring is behind and our data is messy." By lesson 1, what is wrong with it as a diagnosis?
hint: What does a diagnosis do with the dozens of problems every company has?

choices.text: It describes problems where it should propose the approach that answers them
choices.why: The approach is the guiding policy, a separate part. Describing what is going on is exactly the diagnosis's job.

choices.text: It is too short, since a diagnosis carries its incident analysis in full
choices.why: Lesson 3 puts the evidence behind a link. Coreto's diagnosis is three sentences and works.

choices.text: It names four problems and ranks none: the goal list again
choices.why: Right: a diagnosis simplifies, saying which challenge is critical and why the others wait. Four at equal weight is no judgement.

choices.text: It names no team to own the work
choices.why: Owners belong to the coherent actions, the third part. A diagnosis says what is going on.

prompt: A payments start-up's guiding policy reads: "Win small shops on onboarding speed: work that does not shorten the time from sign-up to first payment waits." Which proposal does it rule out?
hint: Apply the lesson's test for a policy: name one sensible proposal it excludes.

choices.text: A redesign of the reports large customers read
choices.why: Right: it does nothing for a small shop's first payment, so it waits. A policy earns its place by excluding sensible work like this.

choices.text: Automating the identity check that now takes two days
choices.why: That shortens the path to the first payment, so the policy pulls it forward.

choices.text: Fixing a bug that blocks the first payment for some new accounts
choices.why: It sits right on the path the policy protects, so it goes first.

choices.text: Removing a mandatory step from the sign-up form
choices.why: Fewer steps means less time to the first payment; the policy favours it.

prompt: Suppose Coreto had formed the Reservations team but never built the load test. By lesson 1's account of coherent actions, what weakens?
hint: Each action makes the others work better. Which ones lean on the load test?

choices.text: The review rule, because reviews of seat-hold changes depend on load-test results
choices.why: The review rule rests on the owner, the Reservations team, and that action happened.

choices.text: The diagnosis, which would have to be rewritten
choices.why: The diagnosis is about where on-sales fail; a missing action does not change what is going on.

choices.text: Little changes, since each of the four stands on its own
choices.why: That describes the first draft, where removing a line changed nothing. The second draft's actions reinforce each other.

choices.text: The debt work loses its measure, and the freeze stays as needed as on day one
choices.why: Right: the load test is what makes the lock work measurable and lets the freeze matter less over time.

prompt: A colleague's sheet multiplies the cloud bill by a growth rate and shows a cost in the millions, with no error on screen. The rate cell holds 15. What happened, and what is the defence lesson 1 gives?
hint: Which of the four mistakes produces no error at all?

choices.text: The rate is text pasted from a document; retype it as a bare number
choices.why: Text in a product gives #VALUE!, an error you would see. This sheet shows a number.

choices.text: It holds 15 where 15% belongs; check one row by hand
choices.why: Right: the quiet mistake. The cell needs 0.15 or 15%, and checking one row by hand is the defence lesson 1 gives.

choices.text: The formula uses a function name from another language; use the local name
choices.why: An unknown function answers #NAME?, which is on the screen. A product needs no function at all.

choices.text: A decimal comma in an English sheet; switch the separator
choices.why: That gives Err:509 in LibreOffice, an error you would see. A whole 15 has no decimal mark.

prompt: A hospital-software company's strategy page has these lines. Match each to what it is in Rumelt's terms.
hint: A checkable claim, an approach that excludes, a commitment with an owner, and a superlative with no mechanism.

pairs.left: Most outages start in the nightly billing batch, which three teams edit and none owns
Billing stability first: nothing joins the batch without a replay test
From May, two engineers from Claims own the batch and review each change to it
Be the most trusted health-software vendor in the region

prompt: An engineering director rewrites the document called "strategy" every quarter, each time a project slips. By lesson 2, what is that document?
hint: When a date slips, which of the four documents moves and which stays?

choices.text: A strategy doing its job, adapting to what happened
choices.why: A strategy changes when the diagnosis changes. A slipped date leaves the diagnosis where it was.

choices.text: A vision, kept current
choices.why: A vision looks years ahead and changes rarely; quarterly rewrites make it a mood, by the lesson's own words.

choices.text: A backlog that has grown too large for one team to keep
choices.why: A backlog covers the next sprints and changes every sprint; this document is quarterly and is about projects.

choices.text: A roadmap under the wrong name
choices.why: Right: the roadmap is the document that absorbs a slipped date. A strategy rewritten every time one slips was the roadmap again.

prompt: You ask three tech leads why a framework migration is missing from this year's plan, and you get three different reasons. What does lesson 2 read into that?
hint: Which check tells a strategy from a roadmap most sharply?

choices.text: There is no strategy above the roadmap
choices.why: Right: a strategy explains an absence with one answer for every team. A roadmap on its own gives a shrug or a different story each time.

choices.text: The migration was badly estimated, and each lead saw a different estimate
choices.why: Estimates explain dates, not absence. The question is why the work is off the plan at all.

choices.text: The vision does not mention front-end technology, so leads fill the gap
choices.why: A good vision names no technology on purpose. The missing piece is the document that says why this and not that.

choices.text: The backlog lacks links from items up to the roadmap
choices.why: A trace column finds orphans, but nothing on a roadmap explains why something is absent; that takes a policy.

prompt: A new director starts writing her teams' backlog items herself. By lesson 2's point about authors, what does the backlog turn into?
hint: A document written by the wrong author drifts towards the wrong question.

choices.text: A list of engineering wishes in date order
choices.why: That is what the lesson predicts for a roadmap drawn up by engineering alone, a different mismatch.

choices.text: A vision, because a director writes about direction
choices.why: The vision belongs to leadership, but writing tickets does not produce one; the horizon stays weeks.

choices.text: A roadmap with tickets in it
choices.why: Right: the lesson's own example. The backlog belongs to the team doing the work, and a director's version carries the roadmap's question.

choices.text: A strategy that changes each sprint
choices.why: A strategy needs a diagnosis and a policy, which tickets do not supply, whoever writes them.

prompt: A Data team roadmap line, "move the nightly reports to a supported database", traces to no strategy action. On inspection, the old database's security updates end next year. Which of lesson 2's outcomes for an orphan fits?
hint: Orphans stop, amend the strategy in the open, or get reclassified honestly.

choices.text: Stop it and move the people to work that traces
choices.why: A database losing support is not optional work; stopping it leaves a risk with a date on it.

choices.text: Label it keeping the lights on
choices.why: Right: it is real, not optional, and it answers to neither strategy. Labelling it as what it is keeps the claims on the roadmap meaningful.

choices.text: Amend the strategy so that this line serves an action
choices.why: Amending is for work that serves something the strategy should have said. This line serves no strategic choice; it keeps a system alive.

choices.text: Link it to action 3, since the replica is also a debt
choices.why: Action 3 is the seat-hold path. An invented link is exactly what the lesson warns makes the column meaningless.

prompt: Put the lines of Coreto's roadmap, derived from the strategy, in quarter order from Q1.
hint: The load test comes before any change to the hold path.
items: Reservations team formed; Platform builds the on-sale load test
Remove row locks from the seat-hold path, measured by the load test
Finish the row locks; automate the deploy freeze before big on-sales
Cloud cost work, off the reservation path
trap: Putting the lock work first skips the evidence the policy demands, and putting cloud cost early ignores that the policy permits it only off the path and outside the on-sale season.

prompt: Another company's strategy page lists four signals under "How we will know". By lesson 3, which one belongs off the list?
hint: A signal should be able to come out false while the outcome is still bad. Which one cannot?

choices.text: Forty design reviews held on the payment path this quarter
choices.why: Right: it counts activity, not effect. Reviews pile up while payments keep failing, so it goes green for the wrong reason.

choices.text: No payment incident during Black Friday week
choices.why: An outcome, and one that comes out false on a given morning; that is what the heading wants.

choices.text: Each change to the payment path carries a replay-test result
choices.why: Evidence that an action is happening, the second kind the lesson asks for, and it arrives before the outcomes.

choices.text: By the end of Q2, the batch takes no table locks
choices.why: Evidence with a date, like Coreto's row-lock line: it comes out false if the work slips.

prompt: A not list says: "We will not adopt Kubernetes." Platform engineers keep arguing about it as if it were permanent. Which of lesson 3's tests does the line fail?
hint: Three tests: somebody wants it, it names the thing, and one more.

choices.text: Somebody reasonable wants it
choices.why: Somebody plainly does, since engineers are arguing for it. That test passes.

choices.text: It names the thing
choices.why: Kubernetes is a precise name; no team can exempt itself by reading it loosely.

choices.text: It is the kind of exclusion better left implicit in the policy
choices.why: Lesson 3 argues the opposite: implicit exclusions get decided by each team separately, and differently.

choices.text: It says how long, or until what
choices.why: Right: a bare no reads as permanent and gets argued with. "Not this year" or a condition tells people when to bring it back.

prompt: Davi talked to Rafaela and to Mateus before the strategy went out, each on their own. By lesson 3, the order for a strategy page is the conversation first, and the ___ after.
hint: What happens to the page once the people affected have heard?

prompt: Which of these practices does lesson 3 give for running the repeat-back test? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think about when, whom, and what to ask.

choices.text: Wait a week or two after the page goes out
choices.why: Right: long enough for the first read to fade, so the answer measures what stayed.

choices.text: Ask "is the strategy clear?" at the all-hands
choices.why: That measures politeness and the relationship with the author, not whether anybody can use the page.

choices.text: Choose people who did not help write it, across teams and levels
choices.why: Right: the authors know it by heart; the test is about everyone else.

choices.text: Give each person the page and ask for a summary
choices.why: The questions are asked without the page, because decisions get made without it in front of anybody.

choices.text: Ask about a situation the page does not mention
choices.why: Right: the third question, and the one that separates understanding from memory.

prompt: Every person you ask answers the first two repeat-back questions in exactly the page's words. What does lesson 3 suggest next?
hint: Recitation and understanding pass different questions.

choices.text: Count it as a pass: the page has clearly landed
choices.why: Exact wording passes the first two questions by memory, which is what the lesson warns about.

choices.text: Ask the third question again, with a different situation
choices.why: Right: recitation passes the first two; applying the policy to a new case is the part only understanding passes.

choices.text: Rewrite the page so that people use their own words
choices.why: The page may be fine; what is missing is evidence that anyone can apply it.

choices.text: Read it aloud again at each planning meeting
choices.why: Davi did that after a round that failed. Here nothing has failed yet; it has not been tested.

prompt: Release after release, a team skips writing rollback scripts for its database migrations because "there is no time". Everyone on it knows how to write one. Which box of Fowler's quadrant is this?
hint: Did they know, and was it a sound loan?

choices.text: Prudent and deliberate
choices.why: A prudent loan comes with a plan to repay. Here the shortcut repeats with no plan at all.

choices.text: Reckless and inadvertent
choices.why: Inadvertent means the team did not know there was a decision. This one knows exactly what it skips.

choices.text: Reckless and deliberate
choices.why: Right: the same shape as Coreto's flaky suite. They know the right way and choose, again and again, not to.

choices.text: Prudent and inadvertent
choices.why: That box is the cost of learning, visible only afterwards. Nothing here is learnt late.

prompt: By lesson 4's list of traces, which of these findings points at a real debt in a loyalty module?
hint: Interest leaves traces in the work, not in anybody's taste.

choices.text: Each change to it needs edits in five other places
choices.why: Right: one change needing edits in many places is a trace of interest, like every venue layout touching the PDF generator.

choices.text: It is written in a style the new hires dislike
choices.why: A preference. It goes nowhere unless it also charges interest.

choices.text: It shows the wrong points balance for some customers
choices.why: A bug, the commonest impostor; it goes to the bug queue and repays nothing when fixed.

choices.text: Its rules differ per partner airline and change each month
choices.why: A hard domain, like the half-price rules: the cost is the problem itself, and no refactoring removes it.

prompt: Match each box of Fowler's quadrant to what lesson 4 says it calls for.
hint: Each box changes what you do next, not only how you pay.

pairs.right: Accept it as the cost of learning, and plan time to rework designs
Write the loan down with a trigger for repayment, and honour it
Change the rule that made the shortcut cheap
Bring in the missing knowledge: review, pairing, hiring

prompt: A team inherits a module a contractor wrote carelessly, able to do better and choosing not to. By lesson 4, what does this kind of code need that a deliberate loan does not?
hint: A loan comes with a repayment plan. What comes with a mess?

choices.text: A repayment date in the register
choices.why: That is what a deliberate loan needs. A mess was never borrowed against anything, so a date alone fixes nothing upstream.

choices.text: Leave it, since careless code charges no interest
choices.why: The lesson says a mess still costs interest, which is why later writers widened the term.

choices.text: A change in how the team works, or it comes back
choices.why: Right: a mess comes with no plan, and the carelessness that made it will make the next one unless the way of working changes.

choices.text: Moving it to the bug queue
choices.why: A bug is wrong behaviour. Careless code may work correctly and still slow every change.

prompt: The engineer who wrote the PDF generator calls it a prudent loan; the engineer who inherited it calls it reckless. What does lesson 4 advise about classifying it?
hint: What happens to a register that reads as a list of culprits?

choices.text: Go with the inheritor, who pays the interest today
choices.why: Paying the interest does not make the payer the witness of how the debt started.

choices.text: Leave it unclassified until the two agree
choices.why: Both describe something real; waiting for agreement leaves the register without the row.

choices.text: Go with the author, since intent decides the box
choices.why: The author's memory counts, and so does what happened after; a plan nobody followed changes the picture.

choices.text: Judge the decision with those who were there
choices.why: Right: the box judges decisions, not people. A register that blames gets no honest answers next time.

prompt: A debt has a principal of 100 hours. Its interest is 10 hours in sprint 1 and rises by 2 hours each sprint after. After which sprint has the running total of interest first passed the principal?
hint: Add 10, 12, 14, 16… until the sum is over 100.

prompt: Put Coreto's four debts in order of interest a sprint, largest first.
hint: Ignore the principal column.
trap: Reading the principal instead puts the replica second, at 200 hours; by interest it is last, at 4 hours a sprint, and the cheap-to-fix suite is second at 14.

prompt: To measure a payments module's interest, a team logs its whole week on the module, new features included. By lesson 5, what does that do to the number?
hint: Which hours would disappear if the debt did?

choices.text: It undercounts, because reviewers' hours are left out
choices.why: Leaving reviewers out is a separate error. The problem here runs the other way.

choices.text: It inflates it with work that would have happened anyway
choices.why: Right: only the extra counts. Counting the wrong thing is what the lesson says breaks the ranking, unlike a factor of two.

choices.text: Little, as interest needs just the order of magnitude
choices.why: The order of magnitude survives an imprecise count, not a count of the wrong thing.

choices.text: It counts the same failure twice
choices.why: Double counting is the trap of adding lost sales to incident hours. Feature work is a different mistake.

prompt: Somebody suspects Davi's 31 hours a sprint for the seat-hold debt is twice the truth. Why does lesson 5 say that error is tolerable?
hint: At 15.5 hours, where would the seat-hold debt rank against the replica?

choices.text: The strategy already chose the seat-hold debt
choices.why: True, and beside the point: the lesson argues the measurement itself stays useful.

choices.text: The CFO reads the yearly reais, not the hours
choices.why: Reais are hours times R$ 150; halving one halves the other.

choices.text: Payback ignores interest
choices.why: Payback is principal divided by interest; it moves directly with it.

choices.text: The ranking survives it
choices.why: Right: the decisions compare debts whose interest differs several times over. At half, the payback goes from 10 to about 21 sprints and the debt still ranks far ahead of the replica's 50.

prompt: A debt sits in a module that will be deleted in four sprints, when its product line closes. Its payback is 8 sprints. By lesson 5's reasoning, what should the team do?
hint: One assumption under every payback is that the interest stays where it is.

choices.text: Leave it: the interest stops before the payback
choices.why: Right: code nobody touches charges nothing, and deleted code charges less. Paying would spend principal to save interest that stops in four sprints.

choices.text: Pay it now, since 8 sprints is a short payback
choices.why: Eight sprints of savings are needed and only four will happen; the payback is never reached.

choices.text: Pay half the principal to halve the interest
choices.why: A half-finished fix removes an uncertain part of the interest, and the module still goes in four sprints.

choices.text: Measure it again in a quarter to check for growth
choices.why: Remeasuring is good practice for code that lives on; this module is gone before a quarter ends.

prompt: A smaller rewrite is proposed: 3 engineers for 6 months at 160 hours a month each, at R$ 150 an hour. Once shipped it saves 40 hours a sprint. How many sprints after shipping does it take to pay back?
hint: Cost in hours divided by hours saved a sprint; the rate cancels out.

prompt: Over eighteen months Coreto's seven teams keep shipping into the old system, so by lesson 6 a rewrite chases a moving ___.
hint: The finish line recedes as the old system changes.

prompt: A vendor will shut down the hosted queue a component runs on in nine months. A replacement queue runs fine beside the old one, and traffic is easy to split by customer. By lessons 6 and 7, what follows?
hint: The ground is going away. Is there an incremental path?

choices.text: A rewrite is forced, since the foundation is ending
choices.why: The foundation ending forces a move, not a rewrite. A rewrite is justified only when old and new cannot run side by side.

choices.text: Move it piece by piece, a slice at a time
choices.why: Right: even when the ground goes, look for the incremental path first, and here it exists.

choices.text: Wait, since standing still for nine months is still an option
choices.why: Once the platform is closing, doing nothing has stopped being one of the options.

choices.text: Case one applies, as nine months is close to a quarter
choices.why: Nine months is three quarters, and case one is about the rewrite's size, not the vendor's deadline.

prompt: Mateus replies that his team is strong enough to avoid what went wrong at Netscape. What does lesson 6 answer?
hint: Are the four failures about people or about the approach?

choices.text: A strong team makes the rewrite safe, if the cutover is rehearsed
choices.why: Rehearsal does not shrink an eighteen-month moving target or the knowledge buried in the old code.

choices.text: Netscape failed for business reasons unrelated to code
choices.why: Spolsky's argument was about the code, not about Netscape in particular.

choices.text: The failures belong to the approach, not the team
choices.why: Right: they catch good teams as surely as weak ones. Knowledge in old code, the second system, the moving target and value at the end do not depend on skill.

choices.text: A strong team should start smaller
choices.why: Starting smaller changes the proposal, not the answer to the claim; the lesson's point is about the approach.

prompt: A team proposes a fourteen-month rewrite of its search service, with a switch that sends traffic back to the old one at any moment. By lesson 6, what is wrong with it?
hint: Both halves of case one matter.

choices.text: Little: a reversible cutover removes the main risk
choices.why: Reversible without small is a long rewrite with an emergency exit, and the exit helps only on the last day.

choices.text: A switch back doubles the cost
choices.why: Keeping the old path running costs something, and the lesson treats it as the useful half of the condition.

choices.text: It still chases a moving target for fourteen months
choices.why: Right: the switch helps only on the last day. Case one needs small and reversible together. The size brings back the moving target and the growing scope.

choices.text: Search is core, so it belongs in the strangler pattern
choices.why: Core and context is lesson 8's question and does not decide whether a rewrite is sound.

prompt: Put these steps of Coreto's migration of one event's seat holds in order.
hint: Nothing moves until there is one place to move it from.
items: Make the seam real: one entry point with hold, confirm and release
Send shadow copies of the event's holds to the new service and compare
Change the event's row in the routing table, before its on-sale
Delete the old seat-hold code and the reconciliation job
trap: Routing before shadowing sends buyers to an answer nobody compared, and deleting is the finish line, not a step to take while any path still uses the old code.

prompt: Which of these were among the paths in the last 10% of Coreto's migration? Choose all that apply.
hint: Rare in traffic, large in work, and often owned by somebody else.

choices.text: Holds the Box Office staff place by hand at the door
choices.why: Right: a path nobody listed at the start, small in traffic and large in work.

choices.text: Events at small venues
choices.why: Those moved first, because a mistake there touched a few hundred seats.

choices.text: Group bookings for schools, holding seats for days
choices.why: Right: they needed a new kind of hold in the service.

choices.text: A partner integration reading the old hold tables
choices.why: Right: it needed a conversation with the partner, under a contract Coreto could not change alone.

choices.text: Big on-sales, after the load test
choices.why: Big on-sales moved once the load test passed, well before the tail; the lesson notes they ran on the new service at 90%.

prompt: Another company plans its strangler migration as "two quarters". By the shape of Coreto's curve, what does lesson 7 say the plan misses, and what habit fixes it?
hint: At the end of month 6 Coreto stood at 71%.

choices.text: The tail; list remaining callers at half the traffic
choices.why: Right: two quarters fitted the bulk and said nothing about the end, and the last 10% took four of twelve months.

choices.text: The first slices, which go slowly; start with the biggest events
choices.why: The first slices are slow on purpose, chosen to be safe. Starting big trades that safety for speed.

choices.text: The seam work, which needs a quarter of its own
choices.why: Coreto's seam took a month; the long part was the end, not the beginning.

choices.text: Shadow traffic, which doubles the timeline
choices.why: Shadow traffic doubles load on the new service, not the calendar.

prompt: Why did Coreto move each event to the new service before its on-sale opened, and not during it?
hint: Where would the event's holds be, halfway through a move?

choices.text: The deploy freeze forbids routing changes in the 24 hours before
choices.why: The freeze is about deploys to the reservation module; a routing row is a different change, and the reason given is the split.

choices.text: The load test runs just between on-sales
choices.why: When the load test runs is not the reason the lesson gives.

choices.text: Venues are told of each move in advance
choices.why: Coreto announced no switch-over to venues at all; the migration was invisible to them.

choices.text: Its holds would be split across two stores in the busiest half-hour
choices.why: Right: routing by event exists so one event's holds stay on one side; a move mid-sale breaks exactly that.

prompt: A director calls the strangler pattern free compared with a rewrite. Which costs does lesson 7 name?
hint: What runs, and for how long, while the migration is under way?

choices.text: A freeze on the other teams' features while the slices move
choices.why: Coreto froze nobody; the teams kept shipping into whichever side owned the case.

choices.text: Running two systems with data in step, until finished
choices.why: Right: cheaper than a rewrite and not free; the work is finished only when the old code is gone.

choices.text: A cutover weekend at the end, as in any rewrite
choices.why: There is no single cutover; the end is a deletion, not a switch.

choices.text: Licences for the routing proxy in front of the old system
choices.why: The facade at Coreto sat at the existing entry point; no licence is mentioned.

prompt: Davi asks the search vendor to cap its yearly rise at 5% instead of 10%. Starting from R$ 9,000 a month in year 1, what would the licence be in year 3, in reais for the year?
hint: Year 1 is twelve months; each later year is the one before times 1.05.

prompt: Put Coreto's three search options in order of their year-1 cost, cheapest first.
hint: Year 1 is the one-off work plus a year of running.
trap: The three-year order puts building second; in year 1 alone adopting (R$ 241,200) edges under building (R$ 246,000), because building's 960 hours land up front.

prompt: A team argues that e-mailing tickets to buyers is critical, so Coreto should build its own e-mail delivery. By lesson 8, what is wrong with the argument?
hint: Think about payroll.

choices.text: Important is the wrong axis; it is critical context
choices.why: Right: the axis is differentiation. Context still needs an owner and a target; it does not need Coreto's engineers building it.

choices.text: E-mail is core, since a buyer with no ticket is a lost sale
choices.why: Losing a sale makes it critical. Core means a venue would choose Coreto for it, and none would.

choices.text: It should be adopted as open source, since that is free
choices.why: Lesson 8 shows adopting was the dearest option for search; free software is not free to run.

choices.text: Building is fine if the team is good at it
choices.why: Whether a team can build something is the wrong first question, the lesson's opening point.

prompt: A health-records company must keep patient data inside its own infrastructure, and needs search over it. By lesson 8's table of reasons, which option does that favour?
hint: Buying puts a copy of the data with somebody else.

choices.text: Buy, with a contract clause forbidding copies
choices.why: A hosted search service holds a copy by how it works; a clause does not change where the index lives.

choices.text: Build, as the data is core
choices.why: Building would mean writing what a search engine already does, which the table names as the shortfall.

choices.text: Whichever is cheapest over three years
choices.why: The constraint removes buying before any sum; money decides among options that meet it.

choices.text: Adopt an open-source engine on its own servers
choices.why: Right: data that is not allowed to leave your infrastructure is the first reason in the table for paying adopting's price.

prompt: Buying search leads building by R$ 88,800 after year 1, R$ 58,800 after year 2 and R$ 16,920 after year 3. Why does the lead shrink?
hint: Compare the two options' running costs from year 2.

choices.text: Integration hours for buying grow each year
choices.why: Integration is 240 hours once, in year 1.

choices.text: The licence rises 10% a year while building runs at R$ 102,000
choices.why: Right: R$ 132,000 then R$ 143,880 for buying against a flat R$ 102,000, and by year 4 the answer flips.

choices.text: Building's database capacity gets cheaper
choices.why: It stays at R$ 3,000 a month in the sheet.

choices.text: The quarter engineer for building is paid just in year 1
choices.why: It is paid every year, R$ 66,000, which is part of the R$ 102,000.

prompt: Suppose Rafaela's time log had shown the self-hosted stack taking 40% of an engineer instead of 60%. With licence R$ 151,200 and integration and exit at zero, what is the self-hosted three-year TCO, in reais?
hint: An engineer-year is R$ 264,000; the horizon is three years.

prompt: A colleague's TCO sheet lists the vendor's invoice in reais and the self-hosted operation as "about 1,000 hours a year". What does lesson 9 say is wrong?
hint: One rule keeps the four lines honest.

choices.text: Operation belongs in the licence line
choices.why: Licence and operation are separate lines; the self-hosted licence is the machines.

choices.text: Hours are not a cost, since the engineers are paid anyway
choices.why: That is the objection the lesson rejects: salaries are paid either way, hours are spent once.

choices.text: It compares money with time
choices.why: Right: every line in hours goes in at the same R$ 150, or hours left as hours look small beside reais.

choices.text: The horizon should be one year for operation
choices.why: The same horizon for every line is the rule; mixing horizons is a second error, not a fix.

prompt: Leaving the hosted service would take 280 hours, while moving to it took 320. Why does lesson 9 put the exit lower?
hint: What does the second move start from?

choices.text: The vendor helps customers move their data out
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so; leverage over the vendor is at signing, not leaving.

choices.text: An exit leaves the people line out of the count
choices.why: The checklist names the people who must learn the replacement as part of the exit.

choices.text: Parallel running is billed once, not per month
choices.why: The month of parallel licence is counted, R$ 7,650, separately from the hours.

choices.text: The team has moved once and has an inventory
choices.why: Right: a team that has done one move, and the inventory of dashboards the first produced. Those two make the second move a little cheaper than the first.

prompt: A year after signing, Coreto re-estimates its exit from the hosted service and finds it has doubled, because teams built many more dashboards in the vendor's own language. What does lesson 9 say a written price gave it?
hint: Compare an exit somebody wrote down with one nobody priced.

choices.text: The chance to see the growth and decide whether it matters
choices.why: Right: a price written down is one somebody watches. An unpriced exit grows unseen and is found on the day it most needs to be small.

choices.text: A reason to leave now, before it grows again
choices.why: Growth is something to notice and decide about, not a verdict to leave.

choices.text: A claim against the vendor for the extra cost
choices.why: The growth came from Coreto's own dashboards; the vendor owes nothing for it.

choices.text: Proof that the TCO was wrong from the start
choices.why: The year-1 estimate was right for year 1; the integration choices since then moved it.

prompt: Including the R$ 49,650 exit did not change Coreto's observability answer. Why does lesson 9 still want the line in every proposal?
hint: What does an absent exit line silently claim?

choices.text: Auditors require it
choices.why: No auditor appears in the lesson; the reason is what a missing row claims.

choices.text: It makes the hosted option look more expensive
choices.why: It does add to hosted's total, and hosted still wins; making an option look worse is not the reason.

choices.text: Leaving it out claims the company will stay
choices.why: Right: it costs one row, and the one decision where that claim turns out false is where the missing row costs the most.

choices.text: Vendors refuse to sign without it
choices.why: The exit is Coreto's own estimate; vendors do not ask for it.

prompt: Leaving a managed message broker would cost R$ 200,000, and an abstraction layer that removes the lock-in would cost R$ 30,000. Above what probability of switching, in percent, does the layer pay for itself?
hint: Break-even probability is portability divided by switching cost.

prompt: By lesson 10, paying for portability is worth it when its price is below the ___ cost of the lock-in it removes.
hint: Probability times switching cost.

prompt: A lock-in would cost three engineer-years to leave, and the team puts the chance of leaving at 2%. The expected cost looks tiny. What does lesson 10 warn?
hint: One caution is about the size of the cost itself.

choices.text: A 2% estimate is too low to be honest
choices.why: The lesson asks how weak a probability is, not that low ones be distrusted on sight.

choices.text: A huge cost stays huge
choices.why: Right: a cost larger than the company finds in a year is not made small by a small chance. Watch the size as well as the expected cost; a lock-in that could sink the company deserves more than a multiplication.

choices.text: Expected cost is a forecast, so budget it
choices.why: It is a weight for comparing decisions, not a forecast of a bill.

choices.text: Accept it, as 2% sits under a break-even point
choices.why: No portability cost is given, so there is no break-even yet, and the size caution comes first.

prompt: With the payment interface in place, leaving the gateway would still cost R$ 30,000. Using a 35% chance of switching, what does a careful sheet compare, and what does it decide?
hint: Portability lowers the switching cost from R$ 135,000 to R$ 30,000; weigh the reduction.

choices.text: R$ 24,000 against R$ 36,750 removed: still pay
choices.why: Right: 35% of (135,000 − 30,000) is R$ 36,750, still above R$ 24,000. The margin narrows and holds.

choices.text: R$ 24,000 against R$ 47,250: pay, since the simplification is harmless
choices.why: The decision stays, but the comparison is the simplified one the lesson says to replace near a break-even.

choices.text: R$ 24,000 against R$ 10,500: accept the lock-in
choices.why: R$ 10,500 is the expected cost left after portability; what portability buys is the difference, not the remainder.

choices.text: R$ 30,000 against R$ 135,000: pay
choices.why: Those are two switching costs; neither is weighted by the probability, and the price of portability is missing.

prompt: A team wraps each cloud service it uses in its own abstraction "to avoid lock-in", with no numbers behind any of it. What does lesson 10 say is wrong?
hint: What does the slogan leave out?

choices.text: Abstractions are a kind of lock-in
choices.why: Every choice locks into something, but the lesson's charge here is paying blind.

choices.text: Proprietary services are cheaper to switch away from
choices.why: The opposite holds: the interface kind of lock-in grows with each direct call.

choices.text: Contracts decide lock-in, not code
choices.why: Interface lock-in is the kind decided in code, and the one a team controls most.

choices.text: It pays blind, for switches that rarely happen
choices.why: Right: without a switching cost and a probability per lock-in, nobody knows where portability earned its price.

prompt: Another company's CFO asks engineering for 10% less and adds: "take it from the cloud, not from people". Its budget has the same shares as Coreto's. By lesson 11's arithmetic, what should the lead tell him?
hint: Compare 10% of the total with the cloud line.

choices.text: Ten percent of the total is about two thirds of the cloud bill, so most of it lands on people anyway
choices.why: Right: with people at 79.0% of the budget, a cut of that size cannot come from the cloud alone, and the lead should say so plainly.

choices.text: A 10% trim of the cloud bill meets the request in full
choices.why: That is 10% of one line, not of the budget. At Coreto's shares, 10% of the total is 68% of the cloud bill.

choices.text: Staging schedules and rightsizing will cover it within a quarter
choices.why: The largest single saving lesson 12 finds is R$ 117,600 a year, 6.8% of a cut that size.

choices.text: Taking 10% from each of the four lines spares people
choices.why: It meets the number and puts 79% of the cut on the people line, the very line the CFO excluded.

prompt: Davi's request for the Reservations team says "Line: People. No new hires." How does that sentence change the decision Otávio is asked to take?
hint: Who pays those four salaries today?

choices.text: The request is now free, so no return needs showing
choices.why: The cost is paid in what those four stop doing, which is why the request still answers "what waits?".

choices.text: Where four already-paid engineers work
choices.why: Right: their R$ 1,056,000 a year is already in the budget, so Otávio decides where they work, not whether to spend.

choices.text: It moves the cost from the people line to tooling
choices.why: Moving engineers between teams leaves the cost on the people line, where it was.

choices.text: It lets the team start mid-year without waiting for the budget round
choices.why: Timing is a separate point in the lesson; the sentence is about what kind of cost this is.

prompt: In July, Rafaela writes a careful request for R$ 200,000 of build machines, in reais a year, against the tooling line, with its return. By the lesson, what works against it that has nothing to do with its content?
hint: When does the competition for money happen?

choices.text: Tooling is the smallest line, so finance gives it no attention
choices.why: Size of the line is not the obstacle the lesson names; a well-written request is read on any line.

choices.text: A request in reais is weaker than one stated in engineer-hours
choices.why: The reverse: the lesson asks for reais a year precisely because that is the budget's unit.

choices.text: Purchases bought outright belong to the cloud line
choices.why: The lesson puts build machines on the tooling line, so the line is named correctly.

choices.text: It asks Otávio to reopen a budget he has already defended
choices.why: Right: mid-year, the same request starts at a disadvantage it would not have had while the budget was being drawn up.

prompt: If Coreto took the whole 10% cut (R$ 1,738,400) from the three lines that are not people — R$ 3,656,000 a year together — what share of those three lines would it remove? One decimal place.
hint: The cut divided by the three lines together.

prompt: Put Coreto's four budget lines in order of size, largest first.
hint: The one with no invoice is the largest.
trap: The usual mistake puts the cloud first because it is the invoice everybody sees; people are 79.0% of the budget and the cloud 14.6%.

prompt: Next year a team adds three staging environments that run all weekend, and the cost per ticket still falls as planned. Why does the unit cost hide them?
hint: Does a staging environment grow with ticket sales?

choices.text: Staging is billed apart from the cloud bill
choices.why: Staging is on the same bill; the lesson found R$ 9,800 a month of it there.

choices.text: Their resources carry Platform's tag, not the team's own
choices.why: Tags decide whose showback line a cost lands on, not whether the unit cost shows it.

choices.text: Coreto counts free tickets in the unit
choices.why: The lesson asks for a definition that stays still; nothing says Coreto changed it.

choices.text: Their fixed cost shrinks per ticket as sales grow
choices.why: Right: a cost that does not grow with sales takes a smaller share of each ticket as sales grow, and becomes harder to see.

prompt: A video-streaming company proposes "cloud cost per server" as its headline unit cost. Which of the lesson's tests does it fail?
hint: What does the company sell?

choices.text: The business does not earn from it
choices.why: Right: a server is an input, and cost per input says nothing about whether the spending was worth it; something like cost per hour watched would.

choices.text: Its definition changes from one quarter to the next
choices.why: A server count is easy to define once and keep; that test passes.

choices.text: The teams have no way to move it
choices.why: Teams move the server count directly with every change they deploy, so that test passes too.

choices.text: It does not survive a change in the provider's pricing
choices.why: A count of servers survives a renamed discount scheme as well as tickets do; the problem is elsewhere.

prompt: Next year's plan has a cloud bill of R$ 236,000 a month for 520,000 tickets a month. What is the cloud cost per ticket sold, in reais, to three decimal places?
hint: The bill divided by the tickets.

prompt: Match each thing Coreto does to the FinOps phase it belongs to.
hint: Seeing, stopping, keeping it stopped.

pairs.left: Publishing the cost per ticket and each team's share every month
Resizing a database sized for a peak long past
Staging off by default, so leaving it on takes an action

prompt: Rafaela wants to wait until every resource carries a tag before showing teams any number, so nobody argues about the split. What does the lesson say?
hint: Approximate, published, corrected.

choices.text: Divide the bill evenly in the meantime
choices.why: An even split is quick and tells every team the same useless number.

choices.text: Publish an approximate split now and correct it in public
choices.why: Right: waiting for perfect labelling means waiting for something that never arrives, and an approximate showback already changes what teams do.

choices.text: Wait, since a wrong number is worse than no number
choices.why: The lesson names this as one of the two wrong ideas that stop showback from starting.

choices.text: Move straight to chargeback so teams tag their resources faster
choices.why: Chargeback needs an allocation every team accepts, which is exactly what is missing here.

prompt: Put the four ways of running Coreto's queue in order of total delay cost, cheapest first.
hint: The parallel run keeps R$ 108,000 a week running for 25 weeks.
trap: The common mistake ranks "highest cost of delay first" as cheapest because it starts with the biggest number; it costs R$ 1,794,000, against R$ 1,728,000 for shortest first and R$ 1,632,000 for CD3. Parallel costs R$ 2,700,000.

prompt: In the Pix-first order, Pix in instalments finishes in week 12 (R$ 48,000 a week), festival seat maps in week 18 (R$ 30,000), the seat-hold fix in week 21 (R$ 18,000) and the partner API in week 25 (R$ 12,000). What is the order's total delay cost, in reais?
hint: Each cost of delay times the week it finishes, added up.

prompt: Another company's queue has item X, at R$ 20,000 a week of delay and 2 weeks of work, and item Y, at R$ 60,000 a week and 10 weeks. Both have a steady cost. By CD3, which goes first?
hint: Divide each cost of delay by its duration.

choices.text: Y, since its weekly cost of delay is three times X's
choices.why: That is the highest-cost-of-delay-first rule, which cost Coreto R$ 162,000 more than CD3.

choices.text: Y, because finishing the long item early frees the team
choices.why: Both orders finish the two items in week 12; what changes is how long each waits.

choices.text: X: its CD3 is R$ 10,000, Y's R$ 6,000
choices.why: Right: making Y wait 2 weeks costs R$ 120,000; making X wait 10 weeks costs R$ 200,000.

choices.text: Neither: the sheet treats the two as a tie
choices.why: Their CD3 figures differ, R$ 10,000 against R$ 6,000, so there is no tie.

prompt: After seeing the R$ 162,000, Júlia says she knows the instalment market is bigger than the estimate assumed. By the lesson, what should happen next?
hint: Is the opportunity cost a verdict?

choices.text: Her knowledge goes into the Pix estimate
choices.why: Right: a higher estimate is what would change the answer; if Pix's CD3 passed R$ 6,000, Pix would lead.

choices.text: Davi holds the CD3 order, because the sheet has decided
choices.why: The lesson calls the argument an invitation to check the inputs, not a verdict.

choices.text: The group splits its time between Pix and the fix
choices.why: Running items in parallel is the most expensive way to do the same work.

choices.text: The dispute goes straight to Helena
choices.why: Escalation is for when the inputs are agreed and the answer is still disputed; here an input is in question.

prompt: The three orders the meeting compared all finish the four items in week 25. What does that mean for comparing their totals?
hint: Same work, same people.

choices.text: The totals are equal, so the choice of order is a matter of taste
choices.why: The totals differ by up to R$ 162,000 between the three orders.

choices.text: CD3 assumes a fixed deadline in week 25
choices.why: CD3 assumes a steady cost each week; a fixed-date item is scheduled, not ranked.

choices.text: The hours priced at R$ 150 decide between them
choices.why: The group is paid the same in every order, which is why the hours are the wrong number for choosing.

choices.text: The totals differ only in how long each item waits
choices.why: Right: the work adds up to 25 weeks in any order, so the delay each item suffers is the whole difference.

prompt: Teams tell Rafaela they lose the first days of every new service wiring logs, alerts and a pipeline. She has two weeks. Which first step fits the thinnest viable platform?
hint: How thin does the book say it can be?

choices.text: A self-service portal with a form for each resource
choices.why: That is the large system built before anybody has used any of it, the failure the idea warns against.

choices.text: One page of agreed setup steps
choices.why: Right: Skelton and Pais point out that the thinnest viable platform is as thin as a page of documentation, and it grows once it is used.

choices.text: A rule that new services use Platform's logging agent
choices.why: A rule measures obedience; the pain was the wiring, which a rule does not remove.

choices.text: A ticket queue where Platform wires each service by hand
choices.why: That is the platform as a queue, which Rafaela was moving away from.

prompt: Catalogue started a service from the template, then edited its pipeline until it no longer accepts the template's updates. Counted by starts, it is on the path. By the lesson, where is it?
hint: Which layer makes a path golden?

choices.text: On the path, since it started from the template
choices.why: Counting only starts misses exactly this drift, which is why Rafaela also asked whether services stay on the path.

choices.text: Off the path in all but name, and Catalogue now owns that pipeline
choices.why: Right: without the template's updates, Platform's promise to keep that layer working no longer reaches it.

choices.text: Breaking a rule, so it should be escalated
choices.why: A pipeline is a golden-path matter, measured and discussed; escalation is for rules such as card data.

choices.text: Still Platform's to fix when it breaks
choices.why: A team that leaves a layer owns that layer, including the night it breaks.

prompt: Platform and the Reservations team meet twice a week to shape the on-sale load test. By Team Topologies, as the lesson reads it, how long should that arrangement last?
hint: Collaboration against consumption as a service.

choices.text: For as long as Reservations owns the seat-hold code
choices.why: A permanent meeting is collaboration as a standing arrangement, which the lesson calls expensive.

choices.text: Until the template carries the load test
choices.why: Rafaela's rule adds a feature to the template once more than one team needs it; the load test has one customer.

choices.text: A few weeks, while the new load test takes shape
choices.why: Right: collaboration suits the weeks while something new is shaped; after that the platform is consumed as a service.

choices.text: Zero weeks; meetings break the product model
choices.why: The book treats a short collaboration as right while something is being shaped.

prompt: A team may leave the golden path, and when it does it ___ what it builds there: the pipeline, the alerts, the upgrades and the night one of them breaks.
hint: Who answers for it from then on.

prompt: A bank's platform team is deciding what to require and what to offer as a golden path. By the lesson's line, which of these should be rules? Choose all that apply.
hint: A right answer, or a better way?

choices.text: Access to production
choices.why: Right: access to production has a right answer and leaving it to preference creates risk for others.

choices.text: Which logging library a service uses
choices.why: There is a cheaper way and a dearer one, and the team that picks the dearer one pays; that is a path.

choices.text: How customers' personal data is stored
choices.why: Right: personal data is on the lesson's rule side, beside card data.

choices.text: Which build pipeline a team runs
choices.why: Pipelines are the lesson's own example of a golden path, measured rather than checked.

prompt: Rafaela kept the portal's read-only version page and gave the deploy buttons a date. What decided which part stayed?
hint: Who opened it, and why?

choices.text: Teams outside the three opened it in their own time
choices.why: Right: use nobody required is the evidence the lesson trusts, and that page had it.

choices.text: It was the part that cost most to build
choices.why: What was spent is sunk and was left out of the comparison on purpose.

choices.text: The three users asked to keep it
choices.why: The three moved onto the template's pipeline; the page stayed for a wider reason.

choices.text: It needs no credentials, no hosting and no security patches
choices.why: It still has to be maintained; the lesson calls it one read-only page to maintain.

prompt: A security team built a secrets dashboard: 900 hours, used by 2 of 30 services six months after launch. It proposes a relaunch with a video tutorial. By Coreto's autopsy, what should it ask first?
hint: Was anybody missing information?

choices.text: Whether the tutorial will reach more engineers this time
choices.why: Promoting harder changed nothing at Coreto, because nobody had stayed away for lack of information.

choices.text: Whether 900 hours justify making it compulsory
choices.why: That lets a sunk cost into the decision and turns a measurement into a mandate.

choices.text: Whether the two users would pay for it
choices.why: Two users' view says nothing about the 28 who stayed away, which is the gap to explain.

choices.text: How the other 28 handle secrets today
choices.why: Right: at Coreto the 38 teams that ignored the portal already deployed on merge; the silent majority is where the answer is.

prompt: The portal was accurate and its rollback worked. What made engineers on teams with pipelines abandon it after one try?
hint: What did it add to a deploy that already ran by itself?

choices.text: An approval step that slowed every production deploy
choices.why: Right: it was the reason engineers gave, a check nobody had asked for on a deploy that was already automatic.

choices.text: Bugs in the version view
choices.why: The autopsy says the version view was accurate; this tool failed without being broken.

choices.text: The guide was hard to find
choices.why: A better guide and a second demo moved nothing, which rules out missing information.

choices.text: Missing permission to deploy to production from a browser
choices.why: The portal held credentials that deploy to production; access was not the problem.

prompt: For the three services that had no pipeline, what does the lesson name as the smallest thing that would have removed their pain?
hint: What did the other 38 already have?

choices.text: A portal with just the deploy button
choices.why: Still a portal, built for three services, with its hosting, patches and on-call.

choices.text: A pipeline from the template
choices.why: Right: it gives them what the other 38 had, deploys on merge, for a fraction of 1,100 hours.

choices.text: A chat command answering which version is in production
choices.why: That was the smallest thing for Platform's own interruptions, a different pain.

choices.text: Faster answers to deploy requests in Platform's channel
choices.why: That keeps them dependent on asking, which is the pain the portal was meant to end.

prompt: Rafaela published the autopsy to the whole engineering organisation, with the cost in it. How does it assign the failure?
hint: Was the portal badly built?

choices.text: To the former Platform lead, who approved the project without asking
choices.why: The autopsy is written without blame; naming one approver would teach people to hide the next one.

choices.text: To the 38 teams that did not give the portal a fair try
choices.why: Those teams already deployed on merge; staying away was a sound choice, not the failure.

choices.text: To the decision to build without asking, not the builders
choices.why: Right: the engineers solved the problem they were given, and the choice of problem was the organisation's.

choices.text: To the engineers, for a tool that was badly built
choices.why: The autopsy says the reverse: the version view was accurate and the rollback worked.

prompt: To cut load at 10:00, an engineer proposes limiting each buyer to six tickets per show during big on-sales. Which of the lesson's marks does it carry most plainly?
hint: Who meets the number six?

choices.text: A default about to be accepted
choices.why: Somebody chose six on purpose here; no library or framework set it.

choices.text: Not a mark: a per-buyer limit is a capacity setting for engineering
choices.why: Capacity is why it was proposed; who it stops is why product decides it.

choices.text: Both options are unsound technically
choices.why: The mark is the reverse: both options sound, and the disagreement is about who bears the cost.

choices.text: A number a user would feel
choices.why: Right: the lesson's own list names a limit on how many tickets one buyer holds; the buyer who wants seven meets it directly.

prompt: Match each way of bringing the seat-hold decision to Júlia to what it does to the decision.
hint: One conceals, one buries, one hands over.

pairs.left: "Shorten the hold or the database falls over"
pairs.right: Hides the trade; product approves what it did not see

pairs.left: A page on lock timeouts and connection pools
pairs.right: Leaves the choice with engineering by default

pairs.left: Options with who feels each, then a recommendation
pairs.right: Puts the choice with the person who owns its outcome

right_distractors: Sends the choice to the CTO for a ruling

prompt: A note to product whose options are built to make one of them win is, by the lesson, the ___ framing again, at greater length.
hint: "We need to shorten the hold or the database will fall over."

prompt: What does the "What would change our mind" paragraph of Davi and Mateus's note tell Júlia?
hint: Whose knowledge is it about?

choices.text: Which option engineering will build if she does not answer
choices.why: The note asks for a decision by a date precisely so the default does not decide.

choices.text: How the hold is implemented in the database
choices.why: The technical content serves the consequences; this paragraph is about evidence, not mechanism.

choices.text: Where her view of the venues outweighs engineering's
choices.why: Right: if venues say a seat lost mid-payment hurts more than a failed on-sale, option A wins, and that is knowledge Júlia has.

choices.text: That engineering will not accept option B
choices.why: Engineering builds whatever she picks; a warning goes on record, not a veto.

prompt: A lead has one afternoon to hunt for disguised product decisions in Coreto's repositories. Which place does the lesson send her to?
hint: Where do defaults and limits live?

choices.text: Database migrations that add indexes to tables
choices.why: Which index a table gets carries none of the five marks; it is engineering's alone.

choices.text: Pull requests that say "tune" or "adjust"
choices.why: Right: along with configuration files, incident fixes and trade-off sections, that is where a new limit or timeout slips in.

choices.text: The test framework's settings
choices.why: The lesson lists the test framework as a choice that carries no mark.

choices.text: Commits whose message mentions a refactor
choices.why: A refactor keeps behaviour as it was by definition, so nobody outside engineering feels it.

prompt: Put these records from Coreto's ADR log in the order they sit in it.
hint: The number is the order written.
items: Seat holds lock rows in the database
No deploys to the reservation module in the 24 hours before a big on-sale
A passing load-test run replaces the deploy freeze
trap: The common mistake puts the row-lock record late because it was written years after the fact; it was written in February, before the others, as ADR-0002, and the freeze, the load test, the new holds and the gate follow as 0003, 0004, 0006 and 0009.

prompt: A team's ADR-0014 has been superseded, and a new engineer wants to give the number 0014 to a fresh record so the log stays short. What does the lesson say?
hint: What do pull requests and incident reports cite?

choices.text: Fine, since the superseded record no longer applies
choices.why: A superseded record still explains how the system came to be, and others still point at it.

choices.text: Fine, provided the title changes too
choices.why: The title is the part that may be improved; the number is the identity.

choices.text: Delete 0014 first so the two do not clash
choices.why: The log is append-only; deleting a record loses the reasoning it kept.

choices.text: No: a number is never reused, or every citation of 0014 would point at the wrong decision
choices.why: Right: the number is what other records, pull requests and incident reports cite.

prompt: A team writes its ADRs after the code has merged, as paperwork at the end of each project. What does the lesson say happens to those records?
hint: One of the ways a log dies.

choices.text: They are more accurate, since the outcome is known
choices.why: Knowing the outcome is what bends the context; the record is meant to keep the terms of the moment.

choices.text: They grow into RFCs of several pages
choices.why: That is a different way a log dies, and it is about length, not timing.

choices.text: Their contexts argue for what was already built
choices.why: Right: written after the fact, the context turns into a case for the code rather than a fair account of the options.

choices.text: They stay sound as long as the five parts are present
choices.why: The parts can all be present and the context still argue for the code.

prompt: The Reservations team proposes adding an approvers section, a diagram slot and a risk matrix to every ADR, so the records look complete. What does the lesson warn?
hint: Why did Nygard keep it to five parts?

choices.text: Records stop being written
choices.why: Right: a short record gets written on the day; a heavy one is put off until the context has gone.

choices.text: Diagrams belong in the decision part
choices.why: The format has no diagram slot on purpose; the concern is how many fields there are.

choices.text: Nygard's format forbids extra sections
choices.why: A team is free to add fields; the lesson's point is the price of adding many.

choices.text: Approvers need listing so the status changes
choices.why: The status changes when the team commits or a later record replaces it, with no approvers field.

prompt: Mateus drafts ADR-0006's decision. By the lesson, what should he leave out of it?
hint: What changes weekly?

choices.text: The venue-by-venue rollout behind a flag
choices.why: The rollout was part of what was decided, so the lesson keeps it in the decision.

choices.text: The load-test run required on each change
choices.why: That rule is part of the decision; reviewers check pull requests against it.

choices.text: The schedule and the engineers' names
choices.why: Right: those belong to the plan, and the plan changes weekly while the record stays as written.

choices.text: The words "We will"
choices.why: The lesson asks for the active voice, "We will…", so a pull request either does it or not.

prompt: A delivery-app company hands engineering a finished spec for live courier tracking, with a launch date promised. During the build, the location service turns out unable to take the update rate. Which of Cagan's risks went untested in discovery?
hint: Can we build it, with this system?

choices.text: Value
choices.why: Customers wanting live tracking was never in doubt here; the system was.

choices.text: Feasibility
choices.why: Right: whether it could be built with this system was the question only engineering could answer, and it was asked after the date was set.

choices.text: Usability
choices.why: Nothing in the story is about whether people could work the screen.

choices.text: Viability for the rest of the business
choices.why: Finance, legal and sales were not where the collision happened.

prompt: On Coreto's shared roadmap, the now, next and later columns are an ___, not a schedule.
hint: They say what comes before what.

prompt: In the on-sale season, Checkout lends its engineering share to product work for one sprint. By Coreto's capacity agreement, what follows?
hint: Lent, then…

choices.text: The share for the rest of the year shrinks by that sprint
choices.why: The agreement treats the sprint as a loan, not as a cut to the share.

choices.text: Product approves the list item by item for the next quarter
choices.why: Product sees and questions the list and does not approve it item by item.

choices.text: Helena has to approve the loan first
choices.why: The agreement lets a team lend for one sprint at a time without a further approval.

choices.text: Repaid next quarter, and recorded
choices.why: Right: every sprint lent is repaid next quarter and written down, so the share survives the season.

prompt: Davi finds that Pix in instalments depends on an engineering theme, a new ledger in Payments, and draws an arrow from the ledger to Pix. Later Júlia wants the arrow removed. By Coreto's rules, who may remove it?
hint: Which theme does the arrow point from?

choices.text: Davi, as author of the theme the arrow points from
choices.why: Right: whoever finds a dependency adds the arrow, and only the author of the theme it points from removes it.

choices.text: Júlia, because the arrow lands in her lane
choices.why: The rule follows where the arrow starts, not where it lands.

choices.text: Either of them, provided both agree
choices.why: Joint agreement is the rule for moving a theme between columns, not for arrows.

choices.text: Helena and the CEO together
choices.why: They hear disagreements the two authors cannot settle; removing an arrow has an owner already.

prompt: What must the tech leads' quarterly report on the engineering share show, by the lesson, so the share is not taken back?
hint: In whose terms?

choices.text: The number of tickets closed inside the share this quarter
choices.why: Tickets closed measure activity, not what the share bought for anybody outside engineering.

choices.text: That the share stayed at exactly one fifth of each sprint
choices.why: The share is reviewed against what it bought; holding a fraction proves nothing.

choices.text: What it bought, such as interest hours removed
choices.why: Right: a share that buys nothing visible is taken back at the first bad quarter; interest hours are a number Júlia plans with.

choices.text: Each engineer's hours on debt
choices.why: Hours spent are the input; the report is about the result.

prompt: Box Office has four engineers, a sprint of ten working days and six focus hours a day per engineer, as Coreto plans. A request is estimated at 72 hours. What share of one Box Office sprint does it take, in percent?
hint: Capacity first: engineers × days × hours.

prompt: A lead is writing "not yet" conditions for three requests. Which of these meet the lesson's test for a checkable condition? Choose all that apply.
hint: Observable, independent of mood, with an owner.

choices.text: When the payment provider's sandbox passes our contract tests
choices.why: Right: anybody looks and sees whether the tests pass.

choices.text: When the team has some breathing room
choices.why: This depends on the speaker's workload, the vague form the lesson rejects.

choices.text: After Box Office moves to the new API, planned to end in June
choices.why: Right: an event in the plan, with a date somebody owns.

choices.text: Once the platform feels stable
choices.why: "Feels" is a mood; nobody else checks it.

prompt: Payments asks Checkout for a two-hour change to the hold logic, to log two extra fields. Capacity is no problem this sprint. By the lesson, what should Mateus check before saying yes?
hint: A request collides in two ways.

choices.text: No check: two hours cost almost no capacity
choices.why: Hours are one collision; the lesson's example of a two-hour change to the hold logic still crosses the policy.

choices.text: Whether it has load-test evidence
choices.why: Right: the guiding policy fences the reservation path, and nothing ships to it without load-test evidence.

choices.text: Whether Payments has priced the change in reais
choices.why: Two hours is R$ 300; the price is not what is at stake here.

choices.text: Whether Payments will lend hours back next sprint
choices.why: Trading hours answers the capacity collision, the one that does not apply here.

prompt: By the lesson, when is a plain no, with no condition attached, the honest answer?
hint: The microservices request.

choices.text: When the asker is junior to the lead
choices.why: Seniority is what a no without a strategy rests on; the lesson moves the reason to the strategy.

choices.text: When the team is fully booked this quarter
choices.why: A booked team has a date when the answer changes, which calls for "not yet".

choices.text: When the request is too large for one sprint
choices.why: Size alone does not decide the shape of the answer; group bookings were 25% of a sprint and got "not yet".

choices.text: When nothing the team could observe this year would change it, short of changing the strategy
choices.why: Right: the microservices migration is on the not-list for this year, so a request to start one gets a no citing the page.

prompt: Mateus's reply ends: "If the festival can't wait for that, it's a decision for you and Helena." Why does a good no name who can overrule it?
hint: Whose trade is it?

choices.text: Taking the cost needs authority over both plans
choices.why: Right: the no is a strategic answer, so overruling it is a strategic decision, taken with the numbers on the table.

choices.text: It shifts the blame to Helena if the festival leaves
choices.why: The lesson names the owner of the decision, not a scapegoat, and Mateus offers to bring the numbers.

choices.text: Mateus has no authority to refuse Júlia
choices.why: He refuses, citing the strategy; naming the overrule is about who takes the cost.

choices.text: Escalation is the standard ending of a no
choices.why: Most noes end with the alternative and the date; escalation is there for when the asker will not wait.

prompt: Twelve big on-sales a year, each failure costing R$ 380,000; the seat-hold fix costs R$ 48,000 once. At what chance of failure per on-sale does one year's expected loss equal the fix? Percent, two decimal places.
hint: The fix divided by the loss if all twelve failed.

prompt: Put the events of Coreto's strategy review in the order they happened.
hint: The slide comes first, and the record comes last.
items: Davi reads the slide's title aloud and stops talking
Otávio asks most of the questions, each answered from earlier work
Helena asks what would make Davi change the strategy
Otávio approves the team and asks for the same slide with real numbers after the season
Davi writes the decision down the same afternoon
trap: The usual mistake puts Helena's question first, as an opening; her two questions come after Otávio's, and hers are the harder ones.

prompt: Another lead's risk: four releases a year, each with a 25% chance of a data-loss incident costing R$ 200,000; the fix costs R$ 50,000 once. How should she put it on her slide, by the lesson?
hint: Expected failures, then expected loss, then the ratio.

choices.text: "One incident this year will cost R$ 200,000"
choices.why: One expected incident is an average; read as a forecast it looks wrong in any year with none or two.

choices.text: R$ 800,000 a year at risk, against a fix of R$ 50,000
choices.why: That is the loss if every release failed, which ignores the 25% and overstates the risk fourfold.

choices.text: R$ 200,000 a year expected, four times the fix, as an average
choices.why: Right: 4 × 25% is one expected incident, R$ 200,000 a year, and the footnote keeps it from being read as a forecast.

choices.text: "The release process is fragile"
choices.why: An adjective loses to every proposal that arrives with a number.

prompt: Why did Davi build the R$ 380,000 cost of a failed on-sale with Otávio's finance team rather than estimate it himself?
hint: Which input is most likely to be argued with?

choices.text: Finance owns the incident log
choices.why: The incident log gives the 8%; the R$ 380,000 comes from refunds, lost fees and venues.

choices.text: Engineers are not allowed to estimate revenue
choices.why: No such rule appears; the point is whose number survives the meeting.

choices.text: Finance's figure is higher, which strengthens the case
choices.why: The lesson asks for a trusted source, not a bigger number; inflating the return spends trust.

choices.text: He will not argue with his own team's number
choices.why: Right: the cost of a failure is the input most open to argument, so it needs a source the reader trusts more than the presenter.

prompt: A colleague suggests putting a simplified version of the row-lock diagram on the strategy slide, so the CFO sees why the fix matters. What does the lesson say?
hint: Consequences or mechanisms?

choices.text: Good, if it replaces the money box
choices.why: The money comparison is the one chart that carries the decision; a diagram would push it off.

choices.text: It goes in the appendix
choices.why: Right: simplified, a mechanism is too technical for the CFO and too vague for the CTO at once; the executive slide is about consequences, and the diagram waits in the appendix for questions.

choices.text: Good, since the slide needs a second chart for context
choices.why: A second chart is a second claim competing for the same glance.

choices.text: Good, as long as its title is a full sentence
choices.why: A full-sentence title does not turn a mechanism into a consequence.
